source_refs.note: Book p. 231: heading 12.3 Continuity and Discontinuity of Functions, printed directly above 12.3.1 with no text of its own; this page carries only our labelled teaching introduction.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The book prints the heading 12.3 and goes straight on to 12.3.1; it has no text of its own here. This short introduction is ours.
So far (12.1 and 12.2) we found \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x)\) by letting \(x\) come close to \(c\) from both sides at the same time. In this section we use limits to answer a very natural question about a graph: does it pass through the point \(x = c\) without a break?

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What the words mean:
A function is continuous at \(x = c\) when its graph runs through \(x = c\) without any break, so that you could draw it there without lifting your pencil.
A function is discontinuous at \(x = c\) when the graph breaks there: it has a hole (a missing point), a jump (the two sides do not meet), or a single point placed away from the rest of the curve.
Everyday picture: the temperature of a room changes smoothly through the day (continuous), but a parking fee that goes from Rs 50 to Rs 100 the moment you pass two hours jumps (discontinuous).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
This section has three steps, each building on the one before:
1. 12.3.1 One-sided limits: the left hand limit \(\lim_{x \to c^{-}} f(x)\) and the right hand limit \(\lim_{x \to c^{+}} f(x)\).
2. 12.3.2 The criterion: \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x)\) exists only when both one-sided limits exist and are equal.
3. 12.3.3 Continuity at a point: \(f(c)\) is defined, \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x)\) exists, and the two are equal.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: You will need two skills from 12.1 and 12.2: finding a limit by substitution (the theorems on limits), and removing a \(\frac{0}{0}\) form by factorising and cancelling the common factor, for example \(\frac{x^{2}-9}{x-3} = x + 3\) when \(x \ne 3\).
